paragraphs.text: This brick of [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) was made from Yunnan leaf in 1990 and spent the decades since in Guangzhou’s tea trade. That is close to where the style began: the pile was devised to give, in weeks, the cup that Guangdong and Hong Kong drinkers knew from raw pu’er aged for years. Yunnan’s state factories brought [wet piling](shou:wet-piling) into production in 1973, after a joint team studied faster piling in Guangdong, so this brick comes from the style’s second decade.

At thirty-six years it is well past the ten that mark [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf keeps changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, which is why its storage has shaped it as much as its age.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.

unsupported.why: Neither the record nor the claims says the style began in or near Guangzhou. The record says the wet-pile method was developed in Yunnan. The claims say Guangdong drinkers were the market and that faster piling was studied in Guangdong, not that the style began there.
